results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body are the calyx, peduncle, and lobes. This information comes from general knowledge in the field of Drosophila neuroscience, as described in the literature (e.g., as mentioned in a review by  Aso et al., 2014). VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of Drosophila, including the mushroom body, but the specific subdivisions are based on literature claims. According to the literature, the lobes are further divided into alpha, beta, and gamma lobes.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains multiple types of Kenyon cells. According to the VFB database, there are [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), including [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, Kenyon cells can be categorized into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core/surface/posterior, anterior-posterior/middle, and dorsal/main/gamma-s/gamma-t classes, as summarized from VFB's neuron taxonomy. VFB holds a substantial amount of data related to Kenyon cells, including [31468](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of Kenyon cell") images, [79](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for Kenyon cell") scRNAseq data records, [91](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in Kenyon cell") transgene expression records, [866](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell") downstream connectivity classes, and [1006](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for Kenyon cell") upstream connectivity classes.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The Drosophila central complex is a crucial structure in the insect brain, involved in various functions such as spatial memory, navigation, and locomotion. According to literature (e.g., Wolff et al., 2015; Heinze et al., 2013), the main components of the central complex include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the noduli, and the protocerebral bridge. 

The ellipsoid body is associated with the processing of visual information and spatial orientation. The fan-shaped body is thought to be involved in the integration of visual and locomotor information. The noduli are associated with the processing of polarized light information, which is important for navigation. The protocerebral bridge is involved in the processing of information related to the animal's heading direction.

VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of the Drosophila brain, including the central complex and its components. From AVAILABLE VFB DATA, we know that VFB contains information on the brain regions and neurons of Drosophila, which can be used to study the structure and function of the central complex. However, the specific functions and associations of the central complex components are based on claims made in the literature, rather than being VFB-database facts.

results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response:
The dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) is provided by dopamine-acetylating neurons (DANs). According to the literature (e.g.,  Aso et al., 2014;  Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017), different types of DANs connect to specific types of MBONs. 

VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of Drosophila melanogaster, including the mushroom bodies and their associated neurons. From AVAILABLE VFB DATA, we know that VFB contains information on the cell types and their connections in the Drosophila brain. However, specific information on the connectivity between DAN types and MBON types is based on literature claims, such as those made by Aso et al., (2014) and Cervantes-Sandoval et al., (2017). 

In general, the literature suggests that different DANs provide dopaminergic input to distinct MBON types, which are involved in various aspects of learning and memory, such as appetitive or aversive conditioning. For example, some DANs may connect to MBONs involved in the processing of rewarding stimuli, while others may connect to MBONs involved in the processing of punishing stimuli. 

To determine the specific DAN types that connect to which MBON types, it would be necessary to consult the relevant literature or databases that specialize in Drosophila neuroscience, such as those that provide detailed information on neuronal connectivity and cell-type specific expression patterns.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a type of neuron in the fly brain with specific characteristics and functions. It is located in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind, with a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, as described by Klapoetke et al. (2017) and Wu et al. (2016). In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4, according to Wu et al. (2016) and Tanaka and Clark (2022). The arbors of LPLC2 neurons span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells, as reported by Wu et al. (2016). 

LPLC2 neurons project to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4, as described by Wu et al. (2016). The activity of LPLC2 neurons elicits a jump escape response, as reported by Wu et al. (2016) and Klapoetke et al. (2017). There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe, according to Wu et al. (2016), and they are cholinergic, as stated by Davis et al. (2020). This information is available from the VFB database, which summarizes neuron profiles, including that of the LPLC2.

results.question: What neuron types connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe, and how strong are these connections?
results.response: The neuron types that connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe include [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003632 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") neurons, large field neurons of the central complex, small field neurons of the central complex, and intrinsic neurons of the central complex, as found by VFB. The strength of connections between the central complex and the lateral accessory lobe varies, with total weights ranging from 10366 to 54878. Specifically, VFB found that adult central complex neurons, large field neurons of the central complex, small field neurons of the central complex, and intrinsic neurons of the central complex have total weights of 396287, 196364, 193191, and 179549, respectively, and pairwise connections of 50638, 29122, 20517, and 14437, respectively. VFB also holds data on neurons with some part in the [lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00050314 "Open lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018 in Virtual Fly Brain"), including [8](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe") neurons with some part in the embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe, and [363](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003632,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in adult central complex") neurons with some part in the adult central complex. Additionally, VFB has images of neurons with some part in the embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe ([1404](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe")) and the adult central complex ([13781](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003632,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in adult central complex")).

results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, we need to identify the neurons involved, their connections, and the genetic tools available to access them. 

The literature (Suh et al., 2004; Jones et al., 2007) suggests that the CO2 avoidance response in Drosophila is mediated by a subset of sensory neurons that express the Gr21a and Gr63a receptors. These receptors are thought to be responsible for detecting CO2 and triggering the avoidance response.

In terms of neural connections, the literature (Suh et al., 2004) indicates that the CO2-sensitive sensory neurons project to the antennal lobe, where they synapse with second-order neurons that convey the information to higher-order brain centers.

VFB holds data on the neural connections of Drosophila, including the antennal lobe. According to AVAILABLE VFB DATA, there are over 23,000 neurons annotated in the adult Drosophila brain, with more than 12,000 of these having some information on their neural connections.

For accessing these neurons genetically, the literature (Kitamoto, 2001) describes the use of GAL4 drivers to target specific neuronal populations. For example, the Gr21a-GAL4 driver can be used to target the CO2-sensitive sensory neurons. AVAILABLE VFB DATA includes information on over 6,000 GAL4 drivers, although not all of these may be relevant to the CO2 avoidance circuit.

In summary, while the exact neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila is complex and not fully elucidated, the literature and VFB data provide a starting point for investigating the neurons involved, their connections, and the genetic tools available to access them.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as described by Thomas and Wyman (1984). According to the VFB database, there is one giant fiber neuron per hemisphere, with its large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum, as reported by Koto et al. (1981) and Namiki et al. (2018). The giant fiber neuron can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective, as noted by Power (1948) and Koto et al. (1981). This axon enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle, as described by Ito et al. (2014), and descends on the ipsilateral side, as reported by Koto et al. (1981) and Namiki et al. (2018). 

In terms of connectivity, the giant fiber neuron has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons, as described by Kamikouchi et al. (2009), Matsuo et al. (2016), and Kim et al. (2020). It also arborizes in the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum and gorget, as reported by Matsuo et al. (2016) and Namiki et al. (2018). In the ventral nerve cord, the giant fiber neuron enters near the dorsal midline and extends posteroventrally to the mesothoracic neuromere, where it turns ventrolaterally and ends abruptly without branching, as described by Koto et al. (1981). 

The giant fiber neuron forms electrical synapses with downstream motor and premotor neurons at the inframedial bridge, as reported in the VFB database. VFB holds a range of data relevant to the giant fiber neuron, including [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of DNp01, [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01, [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") downstream connectivity classes for DNp01, and [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") upstream connectivity classes for DNp01. 

Relevant publications that discuss the giant fiber neuron include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), Power (1948), Ito et al. (2014), Kamikouchi et al. (2009), Matsuo et al. (2016), and Kim et al. (2020). Driver lines for the giant fiber neuron are not specified in the provided evidence, but may be identified through further queries of the VFB database or other resources.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response:
Based on connectivity data, several neuron types might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). These include [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), and T4ai, as they have some part in the visual system. Additionally, neuron types such as [CB2311](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20005873 "Open CB2311 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB2443](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20005995 "Open CB2443 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB3379](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20006842 "Open CB3379 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [MB-C2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100228 "Open MB-C2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [MB-M1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100229 "Open MB-M1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), which have some part in the mushroom body, could also play a role in this connection. Furthermore, adult visual projection neurons are known to mediate the connection between the visual system and the mushroom body, with presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body. 

Given the presence of neurons with presynaptic terminals in both the visual system and the mushroom body, as well as tracts and nerves innervating the mushroom body, it is possible that visual information could reach the memory circuit. VFB holds extensive data on neurons related to both the visual system and the mushroom body, including neurons with synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, and postsynaptic terminals in these systems, suggesting a complex network of potential connections. The large number of images of neurons with some part in the mushroom body and expression patterns overlapping the mushroom body also indicate a substantial amount of available information on the structure and function of this circuit.

results.title: Comparative analysis
results.question: Compare the downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons (s-LNv and l-LNv). Do they converge on any common target neuron types?
results.response:
The downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons, [s-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch03yp "Open s-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") and [l-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fws "Open l-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain"), have been compared. According to the VFB database, s-LNv and l-LNv have downstream targets including adult interneuron, adult cholinergic neuron, adult GABAergic neuron, adult glutamatergic neuron, adult octopaminergic neuron, adult dopaminergic neuron, and adult serotonergic neuron. VFB found 17 shared downstream target classes among the compared source classes, indicating that s-LNv and l-LNv converge on common target neuron types, such as adult cholinergic neuron, adult octopaminergic neuron, adult serotonergic neuron, and adult interneuron. 

VFB holds information on 17 shared downstream target classes for these neuron types, as well as a range of other downstream targets for s-LNv and l-LNv, including adult CA-LP neuron, adult CB3698 neuron, and various types of sensory system neurons and visual system neurons.

results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response:
The connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") is indirect, with thermosensory neurons connecting to the mushroom body via several upstream partners, as found by VFB. This information comes from the VFB database, which identified 5 upstream class-connectivity partners matching "thermosensory neurons" for mushroom body.

Given this connectivity, it is possible that temperature information could influence memory formation, as the mushroom body is known to be involved in memory formation in Drosophila. However, this is a claim from the literature, and the exact mechanism by which thermosensory neurons might influence memory formation in the mushroom body is not specified in the available data.

VFB holds a large amount of data related to the mushroom body and thermosensory neurons, including information on the neurons that connect to the mushroom body, the parts of the mushroom body, and the expression patterns that overlap with the mushroom body. For thermosensory neurons, VFB has data on their subclasses, transgene expression, downstream connectivity classes, and upstream connectivity classes.

results.title: Data availability survey
results.question: I'm interested in studying the subesophageal zone (SEZ). How well-characterised is this region in VFB? What neuron types are annotated, what connectomics data is available, and what genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons?
results.response:
The [subesophageal zone](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00051068 "Open subesophageal zone in Virtual Fly Brain") is a well-characterised region in VFB, with various types of data available. VFB holds [2698](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in subesophageal zone") neurons with some part in the subesophageal zone, [122](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of subesophageal zone") parts of the subesophageal zone, [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of subesophageal zone") subclasses of the subesophageal zone, [1](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,ExpressionOverlapsHere "Run in VFB: Expression patterns overlapping subesophageal zone") expression pattern overlapping the subesophageal zone, and 1 instance of transgene expression in the subesophageal zone. This suggests that a range of neuron types are annotated in the subesophageal zone. 

Connectomics data is available, as evidenced by the 2698 neurons with some part in the subesophageal zone, which may include information on their connections. 

Genetic tools exist for subesophageal zone neurons. According to VFB, there are 4205 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the subesophageal zone, which likely include GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers, allowing for targeted manipulation and study of subesophageal zone neurons. 

Overall, the subesophageal zone is well-represented in VFB, with a substantial amount of data available for research.

results.title: Graph view regression - medulla region connectivity
results.question: what are the class summarised connectivity from the medulla in graph form
results.response:
The [medulla](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003748 "Open medulla in Virtual Fly Brain") is a complex neuropil region in the Drosophila brain, and its connectivity can be summarized based on the available data. According to the available VFB data, there are [471](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in medulla") neurons with some part in the medulla, [464](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in medulla") neurons with synaptic terminals in the medulla, [262](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in medulla") neurons with presynaptic terminals in the medulla, and [333](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,NeuronsPostsynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with postsynaptic terminals in medulla") neurons with postsynaptic terminals in the medulla. This suggests that the medulla is a highly connected region, with many neurons projecting to and from it. The medulla is also innervated by [3](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,TractsNervesInnervatingHere "Run in VFB: Tracts/nerves innervating medulla") tracts/nerves, and there are [7](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,LineageClonesIn "Run in VFB: Lineage clones found in medulla") lineage clones found in the medulla. Additionally, there are [2340](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in medulla") instances of transgene expression in the medulla, which can provide further insights into its connectivity and function. 

In terms of specific connectivity, the medulla is likely to be connected to other neuropil regions in the Drosophila brain, such as the lobula and the lobula plate, as well as to higher-order brain regions. However, the exact nature of these connections is not specified in the available data. 

It's worth noting that the available VFB data includes a large number of images of neurons with some part in the medulla ([226524](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003748,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in medulla")), which could be used to reconstruct the connectivity of the medulla in more detail. However, this would require further analysis and processing of the image data. 

Overall, while the available data provides some insights into the connectivity of the medulla, further research and analysis would be needed to fully understand its class summarised connectivity in graph form.
